Vicente Fox. The Mexican businessman and politician who served as president from 2000 to 2006, becoming the first non-PRI president in seventy-one years. His election marked the end of single-party rule and a democratic transition, though his administration faced economic and security challenges.

Fox rose through the Coca-Cola corporation before entering politics as governor of Guanajuato state from 1995 to 1999. He led the centre-right Partido Acción Nacional—the PAN—to victory in the year 2000 presidential election, breaking the PRI's seven-decade grip on power. He campaigned as a reformer promising economic growth, anti-corruption measures, and modernisation. His presidency saw Mexico's integration deepening through NAFTA, but he faced persistent escalation of drug-related violence and slower-than-promised economic growth. He promoted free-market economics and privatisation, differentiating himself sharply from the PRI's state-interventionist model that had dominated Mexican governance for so long. Fox left office with mixed popularity. His successor, Felipe Calderón, also from the PAN, continued the party's rightward trajectory. Fox's election symbolised Mexico's democratic transition away from the single-party system that Porfirio Díaz had established and that had dominated the twentieth century.
